This bill would keep funding grants that support pay for early childhood education and care workers.
It would amend the Wage Justice for Early Childhood Education and Care Workers (Special Account) Act to extend the special account's operation and the wage increase program.
The extension would run to 30 June 2028 and also aims to improve safety and quality in the sector.
The bill would extend the special account's funding for worker pay until 30 June 2028.
It would extend the Act's sunset provision because payments are made in arrears.
It would ensure the next phase of the wage program supports safe and quality early childhood education and care.
Early childhood education and care workers and families using child care services.

This bill updates the law that protects commercial rights tied to major sporting events in Australia.
It would let event organisers be recognised through a government instrument rather than a new Act each time, with rules set for the Olympic and Paralympic Games.
The bill also sets out what an event must meet to gain protection and how long that protection lasts, and it removes schedules for past events.
The bill replaces the schedule-based recognition model with an instruments-based approach.
The bill introduces requirements for an event to be recognised and limits the protection period.
The bill allows for events to be added and removed by legislative instrument.
The bill repeals schedules for historical events.
Organisers of major sporting events in Australia, particularly those of international significance, and the government bodies that recognise them.

The bill would let the minister declare an exceptional circumstance, such as the ongoing effects of the Middle East conflict, to help businesses respond to situations that are not a national emergency.

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) could then authorise or exempt conduct that serves the public interest but would normally break competition laws, as long as it helps with the response.
The new powers include safeguards to protect consumers, and declarations can be disallowed and will expire after a set period; the bill starts the day after royal assent.
Gives the minister power to make an exceptional circumstance declaration.
Enables the ACCC to authorise or exempt conduct that breaches competition laws if it is in the public interest and assists the response.
Adds safeguards including consumer protection, disallowance, and sunset provisions for declarations.
Businesses responding to exceptional circumstances that are not a national emergency under the NED Act.

The bill would let certain registered nurses prescribe medicines listed on the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme.
The Secretary of the Department of Health could approve eligible nurses as prescribers, suspend or revoke that approval, and the Minister could decide which medicines they may prescribe.
The Professional Services Review would also gain the power to oversee these nurses' prescribing, matching the oversight of other PBS prescribers.
Creates a process for the Secretary to approve eligible registered nurses as authorised nurse prescribers.
Adds authorised nurse prescribers as a new type of PBS prescriber.
Gives the Professional Services Review authority to review PBS prescribing by these nurses.
Allows the Minister to specify which pharmaceutical benefits authorised nurse prescribers may prescribe.
Ensures patients of authorised nurse prescribers can receive PBS prescriptions.
Makes consequential amendments to reflect the new prescriber type.
Endorsed registered nurses who meet specified criteria, their patients, and the Professional Services Review.

Mark Butler I move: That the amendments be disagreed to. This bill is the result of more than 10 years of work—work conducted in a proper, iterative, evidence based way, work that seeks to continue to expand the opportunity for nurses to work at their full scope of practice. Given that there are quite a number of different proposals for the expansion of what we would regard, I think, as the existing work provinces of different parts of the health profession, can I make my view clear that this is best practice. This has been conducted by the nurses board in very close consultation with all relevant groups—medical professionals, patients, colleges and universities. As a result of 10 years of hard work, this endorsement for registered nurses, appropriately qualified, to be able to prescribe medicines has been enthusiastically endorsed by all health ministers in the health ministers group. The Senate has proposed a last-minute amendment to bolt on to this best-practice piece of work, conducted to support the work of our hardworking nurses, a proposal to expand opportunities to podiatrists to prescribe medicines, which reasonable people might think is a good idea in principle. I can indicate that we have been engaging with podiatry groups, including the Australian Podiatry Association, about this issue for endorsed podiatrists. There is a live discussion about whether the sort of expansion for registered nurses that we're seeing now, in the bill that the government presented, should be available to podiatrists as well. But let me be clear; the work in relation to podiatrists is not finished. It is still underway. It is far too early, in my view, to bolt on at the last minute an amendment to expand the opportunity to podiatrists to prescribe PBS medicines when that work has not yet been completed. Unlike the work for podiatrists, the work for registered nurses has been completed. Universities have already started delivering their programs. The Pharmaceutical Benefits Advi

Moved the second reading of the Health Legislation Amendment (Prescribing of Pharmaceutical Benefits) Bill 2025, arguing that it would allow designated registered nurse prescribers to prescribe certain medicines under the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme, improve access and affordability, support rural and regional communities, and reduce pressure on doctors and hospitals. The bill would also apply the Professional Services Review scheme to prescribing.

Argued that the bill would enable suitably qualified registered nurses to prescribe certain Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme medicines, with approval safeguards, and could improve access in rural and regional communities. Supported its passage while urging scrutiny of implementation, patient safety and medicine affordability, and criticising delays in PBS listings and health reform.

Argued for the Health Legislation Amendment (Prescribing of Pharmaceutical Benefits) Bill 2025, saying it would allow suitably qualified registered nurses to prescribe specified PBS medicines under a nationally consistent framework, improve access in regional and remote communities, reduce routine pressure on GPs and emergency departments, and include education, competency and professional safeguards.

Argued that the Health Legislation Amendment (Prescribing of Pharmaceutical Benefits) Bill 2025 would enable qualified registered nurses to prescribe certain PBS medicines, improve access and reduce pressure on hospitals and GPs, particularly in rural and remote communities. Also highlighted the $25 PBS cap, women's health measures and Medicare urgent and mental health services.

Moved amendments to require a trial and review before nurse prescriber treatments could access PBS rebates, arguing that the model needed evidence on safety and effectiveness. Also proposed excluding Schedule 8 medicines, requiring all relevant qualifications and experience, and requiring prescription monitoring and contributions to the National Medicines Record. The amendments were not supported and the bill was agreed to.

Argued that the Health Legislation Amendment (Prescribing of Pharmaceutical Benefits) Bill 2025 would allow eligible registered nurses to prescribe certain PBS medicines under safeguards, improving access especially in rural, regional and remote areas; supported the bill but called for a comprehensive response to the 18 recommendations of the scope-of-practice review.

Supported the Health Legislation Amendment (Prescribing of Pharmaceutical Benefits) Bill 2025, saying nurse prescribing could improve access, reduce costs and ease system pressure with safeguards. Called for podiatrists and podiatric surgeons to receive PBS access within their scope of practice, and foreshadowed moving a second reading amendment.

Debated the Health Legislation Amendment (Prescribing of Pharmaceutical Benefits) Bill 2025. Supporters argued that qualified registered nurses should prescribe specified PBS medicines within training, agreements and oversight to improve access, particularly in rural and remote areas. An opponent questioned diagnostic, medication-safety, consent, accountability and overprescription safeguards, and said the bill would not be supported.

The bill would create a public list of employers who are allowed to sponsor skilled migrants.
The Department of Home Affairs would host the list on its website, showing each sponsor's name, business number, location, how many workers they have sponsored and the jobs those workers do.
The government says this would help temporary skilled migrants find new legitimate sponsors and reduce their risk of exploitation.
Establishes a public register of approved work sponsors.
Requires the register to include sponsor names, Australian Business Numbers, postcodes, numbers of nominated workers and their occupations.
Directs the Department of Home Affairs to maintain the register on its website.
Temporary skilled migrant workers and employers who sponsor them under standard business or accredited sponsorship arrangements.

Moved that the Migration Amendment (Combatting Migrant Exploitation) Bill 2025 be read a second time, arguing it would establish a public register of approved work sponsors, strengthen oversight and transparency, support a targeted temporary skilled work visa program, and protect migrant workers from exploitation.

Opposed the Migration Amendment (Combatting Migrant Exploitation) Bill 2025, arguing that publishing sponsored-worker numbers could expose employers and workers to misuse and that the existing framework is adequate. The debate also described the bill's proposed public sponsor register as a measure to improve transparency, accountability and protection for temporary skilled migrant workers.

Workplace Gender Equality Amendment (Closing the Gender Pay Gap) Bill 2023

The Albanese government is introducing the Workplace Gender Equality Amendment (Closing the Gender Pay Gap) Bill, which will for the first time require businesses with 100 or more employees to publicly report their gender pay gaps, with first reporting planned for early 2024. The Minister noted that women working full time earn 14.1% less than men, costing the economy $51.8 billion annually, and highlighted the government’s broader investment of over $7 billion and reintroduction of gender-responsive budgeting to advance gender equality.
